items.topic: Naltrexone for AUD — opioid antagonist reduces alcohol craving/reward; used with counseling
items.stem: A client with alcohol use disorder is prescribed oral naltrexone with counseling. Which teaching is most accurate?

options.text: Naltrexone is an opioid antagonist that can reduce alcohol craving and block some of the pleasurable effects of drinking; it is used along with counseling/support, not as a standalone cure
Naltrexone works like disulfiram and always causes severe flushing and vomiting after any alcohol
Naltrexone replaces alcohol craving with opioid dependence and should be stopped after one dose
Naltrexone prevents alcohol withdrawal seizures and is the only treatment needed without counseling

rationales.A: Correct. MedlinePlus: naltrexone decreases craving for alcohol and is used with counseling/social support. OpenStax PMH: naltrexone is an opioid antagonist that blocks the pleasurable parts of drinking; adherence and counseling matter.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Disulfiram (not naltrexone) causes the aversive alcohol reaction.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Naltrexone is not an opioid agonist and is not addictive replacement therapy.
rationales.D: Incorrect. It does not treat withdrawal as monotherapy; counseling/support remain part of care.

sources.title: Naltrexone
sources.publisher: MedlinePlus / U.S. National Library of Medicine
sources.evidence: Used along with counseling and social support to help people who have stopped drinking alcohol reduce cravings and help control dependence; works by decreasing the craving for alcohol and blocking the effects of opioids.

sources.title: 19.2 Alcohol Use Disorder
sources.evidence: Naltrexone is an opioid antagonist that blocks opioid receptors and the pleasurable parts of drinking; oral adherence is necessary to avoid relapse; extended-release injectable monthly option exists.

items.topic: NGN matrix — naltrexone AUD teaching indicated vs not
items.stem: For a client prescribed naltrexone for alcohol use disorder, indicate whether each teaching point is Indicated or Not indicated.

rows.text: Explain that naltrexone can reduce alcohol craving and block some of the rewarding effects of drinking

Teach that naltrexone always causes a disulfiram-like vomiting reaction after one sip of beer
Tell the client counseling is unnecessary once the first tablet is swallowed

rationales.R1: Indicated. MedlinePlus/OpenStax: reduces craving and blocks rewarding effects.
rationales.R3: Indicated. MedlinePlus: do not take opioids; high doses while blocked can cause serious harm.
rationales.R4: Not indicated. That describes disulfiram, not naltrexone.
rationales.R5: Not indicated. Counseling/support remain part of treatment.

items.topic: Second-generation antipsychotics — monitor weight/BMI, fasting glucose, and lipids for metabolic syndrome
items.stem: A client starts a second-generation (atypical) antipsychotic. Which monitoring plan best addresses a common class risk?

options.text: Assess weight/BMI and, per orders, fasting glucose and lipids at intervals; teach diet/activity because metabolic syndrome risk (weight gain, insulin resistance, dyslipidemia) is increased
Ignore weight and labs because atypical agents never affect metabolism
Only monitor for agranulocytosis weekly and skip metabolic measures for all atypical agents
Restrict all fluid intake permanently to prevent metabolic syndrome

rationales.A: Correct. OpenStax: metabolic side effects include insulin resistance, hyperglycemia, dyslipidemia, weight gain; nursing interventions include assess weight/BMI, fasting glucose and lipids, educate on diet/exercise. Merck: metabolic syndrome risk is greater with second-generation antipsychotics.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Metabolic effects are a recognized SGA risk.
rationales.C: Incorrect. ANC monitoring is specific to clozapine; metabolic monitoring applies more broadly to SGAs.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Fluid restriction is not the metabolic prevention strategy.

sources.title: Schizophrenia
sources.evidence: Risk of metabolic syndrome (excess abdominal fat, insulin resistance, dyslipidemia, and hypertension) is greater with second-generation antipsychotics than with first-generation antipsychotics; monitor for effectiveness and side effects.

items.topic: Supervised tummy time while awake — supports development and helps prevent positional flat head; sleep on back
items.stem: Parents of a healthy term newborn ask how to balance safe sleep with preventing a flat spot on the baby’s head. Which teaching is best?

options.text: Place the baby on the back to sleep, and provide supervised tummy time when the baby is awake (CPS suggests about 10–15 minutes at least 3 times/day)
Put the baby to sleep prone every night to flatten the tummy instead of the head
Never allow the baby on the tummy while awake because tummy time is unsafe at any age
Leave the baby alone on a soft pillow for unsupervised tummy sleep naps

rationales.A: Correct. CPS Caring for Kids: back sleep for SIDS risk reduction; supervised tummy time when awake 10–15 minutes at least 3 times/day helps prevent flat head and supports development. CDC HIOPS: ensure infants have supervised tummy time every day when awake.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Prone sleep increases SIDS risk.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Supervised awake tummy time is recommended.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Tummy time must be supervised; soft bedding/sleep on tummy is unsafe.

items.topic: Neonatal hypoglycemia prevention — early feeding and skin-to-skin for at-risk newborns; monitor glucose
items.stem: An infant of a diabetic mother is at risk for neonatal hypoglycemia. Which nursing action best supports prevention in the first hours of life?

options.text: Encourage early breastfeeding initiation (within about 30–60 minutes), promote skin-to-skin to reduce cold stress, and follow facility protocol for glucose monitoring of at-risk newborns
Delay the first feed for 12 hours so the infant sleeps uninterrupted
Avoid all glucose checks because asymptomatic term newborns never become hypoglycemic
Place the infant under a cold draft to increase metabolic rate and raise glucose

rationales.A: Correct. OpenStax: encourage breastfeeding within 30–60 minutes, skin-to-skin to prevent cold stress, frequent feeds, and monitoring of at-risk newborns (IDM, SGA/LGA, etc.). Merck: at-risk neonates who are not sick should start early, frequent feedings; high-risk infants often treated preventively.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Delayed feeding increases hypoglycemia risk.
rationales.C: Incorrect. At-risk infants require protocolized screening even before symptoms.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Cold stress depletes glucose stores.

sources.title: 24.2 Care of Common Problems in the Newborn
sources.section: Care of the Newborn with Hypoglycemia
sources.evidence: Encourage breastfeeding initiation within the first 30 to 60 minutes; promote skin-to-skin to prevent cold stress; encourage frequent feeds; monitor at-risk newborns (IDM, SGA, LGA, FGR).

sources.title: Neonatal Hypoglycemia
sources.evidence: Most high-risk neonates are treated preventively; other at-risk neonates who are not sick should be started on early, frequent formula feedings to provide carbohydrates; risk factors include maternal diabetes.

items.topic: DDH — Pavlik harness holds hips abducted/externally rotated; double diapering is ineffective
items.stem: An infant is fitted with a Pavlik harness for developmental dysplasia of the hip (DDH). Which caregiver teaching is correct?

options.text: The harness holds the hips abducted and externally rotated to keep the femoral head in the acetabulum; keep it on as directed by the care team—padded/double diapering alone is not effective treatment
Remove the harness permanently after one hour and rely only on triple diapering
The harness should force the hips into full adduction against the midline
Parents should freely cut and redesign all straps without clinician guidance

rationales.A: Correct. Merck: Pavlik harness holds affected hips abducted and externally rotated; padded diapers and double/triple diapering are not effective. AboutKidsHealth: soft straps keep legs bent up and apart; worn as directed (often nearly continuous early).
rationales.B: Incorrect. Double/triple diapering is ineffective; harness wear follows care-team plan.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Goal is abduction/external rotation, not forced adduction.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Application/adjustment is by/with health professionals; straps are marked.

sources.title: Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip (DDH)
sources.evidence: Treatment is with devices, most commonly the Pavlik harness, which hold the affected hips abducted and externally rotated; padded diapers and double or triple diapering are not effective measures.

items.topic: Medication error/near miss — report via incident report for system learning, not blame
items.stem: A nurse intercepts a wrong-dose medication before administration (near miss). What is the priority leadership/safety action after ensuring the client remains safe?

options.text: Report the near miss/error according to agency policy (incident/event report) so the organization can analyze system factors and improve safety—not to assign personal blame
Hide the event because no harm occurred and reporting is never useful
Document only in a personal diary and never notify the supervisor or safety system
Publicly shame the pharmacist on social media instead of using the event reporting system

rationales.A: Correct. OpenStax Fund 11.3: after ensuring safety and notifying the team, document via incident report; aim is not blame but identifying system issues and continuous improvement. AHRQ PSNet: incident reporting captures events/near misses from frontline staff to detect safety problems for further investigation.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Near misses should be reported for learning.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Use the formal reporting pathway and notify appropriate leaders.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Unprofessional and not a safety system.

sources.title: 11.3 The Medication Administration Process
sources.evidence: Ensure patient safety first; notify manager/charge nurse and provider; document via incident report detailing the error, response, and actions; aim is not to assign blame but to identify system-wide issues and foster continuous quality improvement.

items.topic: Ontario CYFSA — duty to report child under 16 in need of protection directly to children’s aid society
items.stem: An Ontario nurse has reasonable grounds to suspect that a 10-year-old client may be in need of protection because of neglect. What is the nurse’s legal duty?

options.text: Promptly report the suspicion and the information on which it is based directly to a children’s aid society; the nurse must not rely on someone else to report on their behalf
Wait until absolute proof of abuse is obtained in court before telling anyone
Only tell a coworker and assume the coworker will call if they feel like it
Post the child’s identifying details on social media instead of contacting a society

rationales.A: Correct. Ontario CYFSA guidance: anyone with reasonable grounds to suspect a child is/may be in need of protection must promptly report to a children’s aid society; must report directly and not rely on someone else (s.125). CNO: if abuse involves a child/youth, CYFSA requires health professionals to report suspected abuse.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Reasonable grounds to suspect are enough; certainty is not required.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Cannot rely on someone else to report.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Report to a society; protect confidentiality except as required for the report.
